title: Add to your faith (2 Peter 1:5–8)
hookLine: a ladder: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, kindness, love
tomorrow: who keeps you from falling when you can't keep yourself?

cards: In a martial arts gym, the white belt isn't a failure. It's where everyone starts, and nobody expects you to stay there. Is faith the finish line, or only the first step?

A short letter called Second Peter answers with a list that climbs like belts: "Add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge." And it keeps going, rung on rung. Faith, in this letter, is the white belt.

teach.b: Today's question: what does a good life grow?

Here's the whole climb, in the King James: "giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; And to knowledge temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; And to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness charity."
Virtue is goodness that does something. Temperance is self-control. Patience is staying power.
And at the top, charity: love. The verses just before say God's power has already given "all things that pertain unto life and godliness."

teach.h: THE GIFT FIRST, THEN THE CLIMB.
teach.b: So the gift comes first, and the climb answers it, with real effort.
A neighbor tradition keeps a list like this too.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna the marks of a person born to a divine nature: fearlessness, generosity, self-control, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion for all beings, gentleness, forgiveness, steadiness.
What's shared is the shape: a good life isn't one feeling, it's qualities grown side by side, self-control and gentleness among them.
And the honest difference: Second Peter's ladder stands on faith in Christ and climbs to love at the top. The Gita's list belongs to Krishna's teaching on two natures and the path toward freedom.

how: Christians read 2 Peter 1:5–8 as a picture of growing in faith over a lifetime, and some study groups take one virtue from the list at a time.

games.q: what does “add to your faith” mean?
o: add good deeds to earn your way into faith
add more prayers until God says yes
build virtues on top of faith, rung by rung

games.q: the climb in 2 Peter — tap the pairs.

s: in 2 Peter, faith is the top of the ladder
faith is the ground floor; the climb ends in charity, love.
2 Peter says the power for the climb is already given
all things that pertain unto life and godliness.
the Gita and 2 Peter teach the same path
they share some virtues, like self-control and gentleness, but start and end in different places.

games.q: your Hindu friend's grandmother keeps a list of virtues from the Bhagavad Gita by her mirror, and you spot self-control and gentleness on it. what's fair to say?
o: it's the same list, so the two faiths are the same.
both grow virtues side by side, from different ground.
hers is just rules; only one list is about the heart.
games.why: both lists treat a good life as qualities grown together. 2 Peter's stands on faith in Christ and ends in love; the Gita's belongs to Krishna's teaching on the path to freedom.

practice: Run through the rungs: virtue, knowledge, self-control, patience, godliness, kindness, love, and pick the one that seems next for you. Name the wish: one real step on that rung. Name what usually trips you there.
Then decide on one small thing you'll do the moment that obstacle shows up.

wordCard.voice: Add to your faith. Second Peter, chapter one: a climb from faith through virtue, knowledge and patience, all the way up to love.

orig.note: Greek: virtue, excellence. 2 Peter 1:5, add to your faith virtue.

carryVoice: Your line: add to your faith. The first rung is a start, not a finish. Go gently.
